# A macro whose configured branches compute one result is ported once

Status: `open`: the change is crustify `769d102` on `libgit2-crustify/evolution/config-branches-of-one-result`, made on
2026-11-14 after the triage of open proposals, awaiting its review.

Goal: Idiomatic Rust, and Least constraint: a shim where the Rust can state the result is a
constraint without a reason.

## Signal

A rule an agent had to work out by hand that a skill should have stated.

## Evidence

`wave-225/batch-0/run-1` ported `mac::p_strnlen` (`src/util/strnlen.h`). The header defines
it by platform: `#define p_strnlen strnlen` (libc's), or, under `NO_STRNLEN` (MinGW, Solaris,
Apple, MidnightBSD, old MSVC), a `GIT_INLINE` body over `memchr(s, 0, maxlen)`. Both give
the offset of the first NUL within `maxlen`, or `maxlen`, for every input.

`binding-symbols`' Macros section reaches "a macro whose expansion depends on the build's
configuration" through a shim, `crustify_<NAME>`, and binds a symbol alias "through the safe
wrapper of the symbol it names". `porting-symbols`' Macros section defers to it. Read
literally, the port would be a shim over libc's `strnlen`, or a wrapper of it, though
`dependencies.json` gives libc's `strnlen` the `std` route and nothing of its state is
shared with C. The task message had to settle it: "Port what this build defines, and say in
its docs what the other branch is." The batch ported a native `const fn strnlen(&[u8])`, by
`CStr::from_bytes_until_nul`, and documented the `NO_STRNLEN` branch on it.

The module pass, `wave-225/batch-1/run-1`, judged the port against `porting-symbols`'
Macros section and filed no finding: the body computes on its arguments alone, so it takes
the `const` function form, and libc's `strnlen` is reached by its `std` route. The reading
the shim exception invites is unclear twice over: what selects the branch here is the
target platform (`__APPLE__`, `__sun`, `__MINGW32__`, `__MidnightBSD__`, `_MSC_VER`), which
Rust's own `cfg(target_os, target_env)` does see, and a port reimplements the body instead
of reaching the C's expansion, so a shim over the C would make the port a binding. The
section should say which configurations the exception means, and that it applies only
where the branches differ in what they compute.

## Destination

The spec: `porting-symbols`' Macros section.

## Change

Add, after its first paragraph:

> A macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration is ported once when every
> configuration's expansion computes the same result for every input, its documentation
> naming the branches the build does not take; only one whose branches differ in what they
> compute keeps `binding-symbols`' shim. A symbol alias of an out-of-tree library's entity
> is ported as that entity's route reaches it, as `dependencies`' Confirmation section
> checks it: through the standard library, it is a native function.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |

## Validation

`wave-225/batch-0`'s tests: its unit tests check every NUL position in every bound up to 70

---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

# Porting symbols

How a scheduled C symbol is reimplemented in safe Rust: the symbol route, which follows
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section and starts from
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s; the types it reaches are
[`porting-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s.

A ported symbol's implementation is translated to safe, idiomatic Rust with its observable
behaviour preserved.

## 1. Functions

A ported function takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Functions
section gives a function, or keeps its wrapper's, as [`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes.

A function no wrapper gives an API yet, whose body only reads or writes one member, or only
returns a value an existing item of its own module's safe API already gives, is ported as
that item, so that the port writes no second API: the accessor or method carries the
function's `Replaces` anchor and alias beside its own. Its export, where remaining C calls
it, is written in the module's gateway, over that item.

A function that remaining C calls or takes the address of is exported, as
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes. Its gateway undoes what the safe API converted,
so that its C callers see what the C function did: it rebuilds the safe arguments from the
C ones, writes the out-parameters and buffers through the pointers C passed, and reports a
failure through the function's C error convention, its return and the error state the C
function set, `errno` included, which the Rust behind it never sets. A panic is caught at
the gateway and reported as a failure, or aborts where the function cannot fail: none
unwinds into C. The gateway checks each export against the raw binding of the C declaration
it replaces, as [`testing-gates`](../../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions
section asks, in a constant the compiler evaluates, `const _: () = { let _ = [sys::<name>,
<name>]; };`, whose two function items coerce to one function-pointer type only where their
signatures agree; the binding is allowlisted for it where the bindings lack it. A variadic function's export cannot be defined on stable Rust, so a shim
keeps its C signature, as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, and calls
a fixed-arity export with the arguments it formats or unpacks. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the
export, with the raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it and its declaration in its
header, once no remaining C references it. C that only a configuration the target is built
without compiles, such as another platform's, is no remaining C: like a test case
configured out, as [`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Tests
follow their modules section describes, it holds no export back, and a build under that
configuration meets the function undeclared where it calls it.

A lifecycle routine's port reimplements it behind the policy its type's port or wrap
wrote, which it repoints at the Rust routine, and writes no API of its own, as `binding-types`'
Lifecycle section has the symbol route skip what a type batch emitted. The last of its
type's own module's memory users to be ported moves its storage to Rust's allocator,
unless C of other modules still allocates or frees it raw, which leaves that move to its
`port/memory`.

## 2. Globals

A ported global takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Globals section gives a global, or keeps its wrapper's. Rust holds its storage from its
port, beside its module's C, which keeps its own copy until the switch; from then on
the Rust's is the only one. A global that remaining C accesses
is exported, as a function is, and keeps the C layout and the synchronization protocol
those accesses rely on while it is. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the export, as
a function's does, and its storage then takes a native form, as state moved out of C does.
A thread-local one cannot be defined for C on stable Rust, so a shim keeps its C definition,
as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, until that stage. A global no
remaining C accesses is native from its port.

## 3. Function pointers

A ported function pointer keeps the safe callable type
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section gives it, which is its API from its port: its Rust consumers, and
the ported code that calls it, use that type alone. While remaining C calls a function
pointer of its type or supplies one, its C form stays beneath it: the function-pointer type
of its raw binding, the trampolines through which a Rust closure reaches the C that calls
it, and the `unsafe` constructor through which a C function reaches Rust, passed to an
export, whose gateway builds the C variant from the function and the context it receives,
or stored where C wrote it. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes that C form, with the
raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it, once no remaining C references it, as
[`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section times it. A

implementation too: its closure or trait alone.

`port/unexport`, even when Rust alone implements it, so that the deferred public C API, as
[`conventions`](../../conventions/SKILL.md)'s Exports section describes, can let C
implement it again.

## 4. Static inline functions

A `static inline` function a header defines is internal API of the module the
decomposition gives it, and is ported as its other functions are. Its C callers expand its
body in their own TUs, so an export alone does not reach them: at the module's
switch, the header's definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C
calls the Rust module's export, under the function's bare name, where it inlined the body.
<!-- TODO: cross-language LTO (`-Clinker-plugin-lto`, with a clang whose LLVM matches
rustc's) would inline the export back into its C callers. -->

## 5. Macros

A macro takes the Rust form [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section gives it,

goes with its TU. A macro a header defines, internal or public API that another module's C
may expand, also stays in its header for the remaining C, unexported, and its C and Rust
forms are not linked, beyond the Rust form's annotation. It keeps expanding where remaining C
invokes it, until its header goes with the last C file that includes it, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes: a type generator keeps minting the instances its remaining invocations define,
and what an expansion calls or accesses is reached as any remaining C reaches it, a
function or global Rust owns through its export, a type through its C layout. An
expansion site is a use by the function that holds it, so it holds back the later stages
of what it reaches, as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section counts its users.

---
name: dependencies
description: "How a campaign reaches libraries from outside its tree: the order of routes, adopted crates and their criteria, local bindings, wrappers, side campaigns, sources, reuse. Read before planning an out-of-tree library's route, or advancing its wrapper or a fork of an adopted crate."
---

# Dependencies

How a campaign reaches the libraries its target uses from outside its tree: libc, zlib,
OpenSSL and the like. The [decomposition](../decomposition/SKILL.md) records each one a module
uses as a dependency record, counting the entities the module consumes from it, and
`dependencies.json` records each library once: the release the target links, its source,
its crustify campaign, the Rust crates that port or bind it, and every entity the
campaign uses of it, mapped to what those crates offer, as
[`dependencies-schema`](../../artifacts/dependencies-schema/SKILL.md) describes. This spec describes
what the campaign does with them.

## 1. Routes

What a campaign uses of an out-of-tree library is reached, in this order of preference:

1. through the Rust standard library, wherever no state is shared with C, as
   [Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) describes;
2. through established crates adopted for parts of the library, extended in a fork where
   they lack a little, as [Adopted crates](#6-adopted-crates) describes;
3. bound locally, in the consuming module's own `ffi_import` region over the library's
   established `-sys` crate, such as `libc`, for what is left too small to be worth a
   wrapper, as [Local bindings](#7-local-bindings) describes; and
4. through the library's crustify campaign, a wrap campaign of its own whose crate is the
   library's Crustify wrapper, as the rest of this section and
   [Side campaigns](#3-side-campaigns) describe.

The routes are named `std`, `crate`, `local` and `crustify-campaign` in
`dependencies.json`. The plan records each library's candidate crates, each with its
quality assessment, and maps every entity the campaign uses of the library to what each
candidate and the standard library offer for it, recommending a route for each entity and,
from those, the crates to adopt and the route of what they leave uncovered. Once the plan is
complete, the recommendation is put to the user, who chooses per library, and the choice
is recorded as the library's `decision`, as
[`dependencies-schema`](../../artifacts/dependencies-schema/SKILL.md) describes. The
records inform the choice; they do not make it. Each entity's route is then checked against
the code by the first batch that needs it, as [Confirmation](#8-confirmation) describes.

A library's wrapper is a wrap campaign of the source it is built from, in a repository of
its own: `<source>-crustify` under the `crustify-rs` organization, `<source>` being the
name of that source's repository, named and laid out as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section and [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s
Tree section describe for any wrap campaign, so that a later campaign whose target is the
source itself continues it. The libraries one source builds share its wrapper, each a link
unit of it: OpenSSL's `libcrypto` and `libssl` are both wrapped in `openssl-crustify`.
It is cloned beside the campaign's repository, as `../<source>-crustify`, never inside
it. The campaign's workspace depends on its crate by
Git, pinned to a commit, with a Cargo `[patch]` pointing at the clone while the campaign
extends it; the parent campaign's safe crate, its raw bindings included, names its safe
wrappers, never its raw bindings once a safe wrapper exists.

A wrapper covers only what the campaigns that use it reach through it: the entities
their waves need through the wrapper rather than the standard library, wrapped as those
waves need them. It exposes its own safe
types, with no conversions to or from the types of other crates that wrap the same
library.

## 2. Standard-library equivalents

The campaign's Rust reaches an out-of-tree library's entity through the Rust standard
library wherever the state the entity works on stays in Rust, or crosses to C only as
values the boundary converts, and through the library's wrapper wherever that state is
shared with C, as [`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section describes. The plan recommends which for each entity, from what it knows of the
uses; the batch that first needs the entity judges it from the code, as
[Confirmation](#8-confirmation) describes, so a wrapper covers what the campaign's Rust
reaches through it as its waves need it.

## 3. Side campaigns

A wrapper's work is a side campaign, continued in its own repository: it keeps its own
settings, plan, schedule, branches, builds and accounting there, and its batches land on
its own wave branches, as any wrap campaign's do. Its scope is what the parent campaign
reaches through the wrapper, not the whole library, and it grows as the parent's waves
need more of it. Its settings are the parent's, but for its `campaign`, which is `wrap`, its
`source`, the library at the release the target links, and its `scope`; a settings change
the parent applies is applied to its side campaigns too.

The side campaign advances at the parent's pace. Before a parent wave starts, the
entities its items need through each library's wrapper are judged from the items, the
libraries their modules' `depends_on.external` records name and the entities they use:
every entity of a library the standard library does not replace, and of the others those
whose state the items share with the remaining C, as
[Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) describes. What the
wrapper lacks of them, the side campaign plans and runs waves to wrap; once those are
promoted to its working branch, the parent's pin, its library's `crustify_campaign.pin`
in `dependencies.json`, moves to that commit, and the parent wave starts. A batch that needs
an entity through a wrapper that lacks it reports it rather than reaching it through raw
bindings, and runs again once the side campaign has wrapped it. The parent ships
only once each wrapper it pins has shipped the commit it pins, each with the user's
approval.

Each wrapper's crate bundles its own raw bindings, generated from the library's headers,
as [`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes. While its `c/` is the whole
library, the crate builds by default in system mode, linking the system's copy, as the
other crates of a dependent's build that wrap the same library do, so that a process holds
one copy of it; its version check accepts any release ABI-compatible with the one its
bindings were generated from, which shares its soname. Once its side campaign has ported
part of the library, the crate bundles the C that remains, with its symbols prefixed, so
that it never collides with another copy of the library in the same process, and passes
the prefix to the C builds of the campaigns that depend on it, as the raw bindings'
Generation section describes.

## 4. Sources

A library the target links from the system has no
source of the campaign's own, so its side campaign's `c/` is the library's upstream
repository at the release the target was built against: the version its build resolved,
as its build system reports it (CMake's found version, `pkg-config --modversion`), the
system package that provides it, or, for a library built from source, its own version
header. The distribution's patches to that release, if any, are recorded beside it, in the
library's `resolved` and `source` in `dependencies.json`.

The side campaign builds and installs the library locally, once per build variant of its
parent, under its own `crustify/builds/<variant>/install`, so that each variant of the
target links the library built with the same instrumentation; a sanitizer that instruments
every component, MSan among them, needs it. The parent's variants are then rebuilt against
those installs, as the setup workflow's Builds section describes.

libc is the exception. Every other library on the system, and the dynamic loader, depend
on the system's glibc, so the target keeps linking it, and its side campaign's `c/` holds
glibc's source at the installed version, for reading its behaviour. Its raw bindings, like
any wrapper's, are generated from the host's headers, which are that glibc's, so layouts and
constants that differ between architectures, such as `struct stat`, are the campaign
target's.

## 5. Reuse

Before a campaign creates a library's wrapper, it checks `crustify-rs` for
`<source>-crustify`. One that exists is cloned and its side campaign continued: what it
already wraps is not scheduled again, and only what it lacks is planned, as additions to
its own plan. A library without one gets a new repository, created once the user approves,
which every later campaign that uses the library continues.

## 6. Adopted crates

A crate is adopted for a coherent part of what the campaign uses of a library, the
entities a subsystem, a header's API or a kind of resource (sockets, memory maps,
processes) groups, never for an item or two: entities that share state, such as a stream's
initializer, its operations and its finalizer, take the same crate. A library may be
covered by several crates, the fewest that cover what the campaign uses: libc's uses may
be the standard library's for files and threads, one crate's for sockets and another's for
the remaining system calls. What no adopted crate covers takes the next route.

Each entity's `matches` record what each candidate offers for it, and how closely; each
candidate's `quality_assessment` weighs it, in prose, on the considerations below. Only
soundness and advisories are gates: a crate with undefined behaviour reachable from its
safe API, or with an unfixed advisory on what the campaign uses, is not adopted unless a
fork fixes it. The others are weighed against the alternative routes, which are never free:
a crustify campaign or local bindings put the campaign's own unsafe code where the crate
would have put none.

- **coverage**: it serves what the campaign uses of those entities, as their `matches`
  show. Same behaviour is not required: a port is a new implementation, and a difference
  the port can absorb in its own safe code (a verifier, a loop in place of a sizing call,
  configuration loaded eagerly), or that it can adopt deliberately and record as the safe
  API's changed behaviour (an option it rejects, a deprecated fallback it drops), weighs
  against the crate only by its cost. What only an extension of the crate would provide
  is extended, as below;
- **shared state**: where the remaining C shares an entity's state with the Rust, such as
  a handle the C still uses, the crate exposes that state to C, which the entity's match
  note says, citing the release point after which the C stops sharing it. A crate that
  binds the C library and exposes its raw handles can; one that reimplements the library
  serves only where no state crosses to the remaining C, as
  [Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) describes. An entity
  only one module uses, whose port keeps the state in Rust, shares none;
- **soundness** (a gate): a read of its public API and its unsafe code finds no undefined
  behaviour reachable from its safe API, by the hazards
  [`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary excludes from the campaign's
  own; a deterministic scan of its unsafe surface backs the judgement where that surface
  is large or the judgement is borderline;
- **advisories** (a gate): no unfixed security advisory affects the version and the
  features the campaign uses; and
- **maintenance**: how likely the crate is to keep up with its dependencies, toolchains and
  advisories: its release history and its maintainers, weighed by how much the crate does
  and how settled its scope is, since a complete crate with a narrow scope needs few
  releases. A crate whose `-sys` crate the alternative route would use anyway is no
  riskier than that route. Its license and minimum Rust version suit the campaign's.

Every crate that passes the gates and weighs better than the alternative routes is
recommended for the entities it serves best. Once the user adopts it,
those entities get no wrapper and no batches: their consumers use the crate directly, and
their bindings name its types and functions where they would name the wrapper's.

A crate that lacks a little of what it is adopted for is extended rather than passed over: in a fork
cloned beside the campaign's repository, as a wrapper is, on a branch of its own, which the
campaign's workspace pins with a Cargo `[patch]`. The extension is offered upstream, as a
pull request opened with the user's approval, so that the fork can be dropped once it is
merged.
<!-- TODO: whether a ship point may pin an unmerged fork is decided at the end of the
first campaign that meets one. -->

## 7. Local bindings

What a library's adopted crates leave uncovered, when it is too small to be worth a
wrapper, a few functions, is bound where it is used: over the library's established `-sys` crate, in
the consuming module's `ffi_import` region, behind a safe API of that module's, as
[`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md) describes for any item, by the batch that consumes
it. What grows past a few functions, or what several modules need, is the library's
crustify campaign's.

## 8. Confirmation

An entity's route is a recommendation made before any of its uses was translated. The first
batch that binds or ports one of its users checks the route against the code it translates,
by the uses the entity's `match` and note describe, and reports what it found in its final
message, which is recorded as the entity's `confirmation`. Each later batch takes
the confirmed route.

When the route does not hold, the batch reaches the entity through another route the
library's `decision` already allows, in this order: the standard library, where
[Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) allows it; another crate the
decision adopts for the library; the decision's `uncovered` route. A `crustify-campaign`
route that the library's crustify campaign does not yet cover is reported, and advanced as
[Side campaigns](#3-side-campaigns) describes, before the batch runs again. Where no route
the decision allows serves the entity, because the library leaves nothing `uncovered` or
only a crate the user has not adopted would, the batch reports it, and it is put
to the user, whose answer is recorded among the decision's `overrides`.

What a campaign uses of an out-of-tree library is reached, in this order of preference:

1. through the Rust standard library, wherever no state is shared with C, as
   [Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) describes;
2. through established crates adopted for parts of the library, extended in a fork where
   they lack a little, as [Adopted crates](#6-adopted-crates) describes;
3. bound locally, in the consuming module's own `ffi_import` region over the library's
   established `-sys` crate, such as `libc`, for what is left too small to be worth a
   wrapper, as [Local bindings](#7-local-bindings) describes; and

   library's Crustify wrapper, as the rest of this section and

quality assessment, and maps every entity the campaign uses of the library to what each
candidate and the standard library offer for it, recommending a route for each entity and,

the code by the first batch that needs it, as [Confirmation](#8-confirmation) describes.

its own: `<source>-crustify` under the `crustify-rs` organization, `<source>` being the
name of that source's repository, named and laid out as

unit of it: OpenSSL's `libcrypto` and `libssl` are both wrapped in `openssl-crustify`.

it. The campaign's workspace depends on its crate by
Git, pinned to a commit, with a Cargo `[patch]` pointing at the clone while the campaign
extends it; the parent campaign's safe crate, its raw bindings included, names its safe
wrappers, never its raw bindings once a safe wrapper exists.

A wrapper covers only what the campaigns that use it reach through it: the entities
their waves need through the wrapper rather than the standard library, wrapped as those
waves need them. It exposes its own safe
types, with no conversions to or from the types of other crates that wrap the same
library.

The campaign's Rust reaches an out-of-tree library's entity through the Rust standard
library wherever the state the entity works on stays in Rust, or crosses to C only as
values the boundary converts, and through the library's wrapper wherever that state is
shared with C, as [`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section describes. The plan recommends which for each entity, from what it knows of the
uses; the batch that first needs the entity judges it from the code, as
[Confirmation](#8-confirmation) describes, so a wrapper covers what the campaign's Rust
reaches through it as its waves need it.

## 3. Side campaigns

A wrapper's work is a side campaign, continued in its own repository: it keeps its own
settings, plan, schedule, branches, builds and accounting there, and its batches land on
its own wave branches, as any wrap campaign's do. Its scope is what the parent campaign
reaches through the wrapper, not the whole library, and it grows as the parent's waves
need more of it. Its settings are the parent's, but for its `campaign`, which is `wrap`, its
`source`, the library at the release the target links, and its `scope`; a settings change
the parent applies is applied to its side campaigns too.

The side campaign advances at the parent's pace. Before a parent wave starts, the
entities its items need through each library's wrapper are judged from the items, the
libraries their modules' `depends_on.external` records name and the entities they use:
every entity of a library the standard library does not replace, and of the others those
whose state the items share with the remaining C, as
[Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) describes. What the
wrapper lacks of them, the side campaign plans and runs waves to wrap; once those are
promoted to its working branch, the parent's pin, its library's `crustify_campaign.pin`
in `dependencies.json`, moves to that commit, and the parent wave starts. A batch that needs
an entity through a wrapper that lacks it reports it rather than reaching it through raw
bindings, and runs again once the side campaign has wrapped it. The parent ships
only once each wrapper it pins has shipped the commit it pins, each with the user's
approval.

Each wrapper's crate bundles its own raw bindings, generated from the library's headers,
as [`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes. While its `c/` is the whole
library, the crate builds by default in system mode, linking the system's copy, as the
other crates of a dependent's build that wrap the same library do, so that a process holds
one copy of it; its version check accepts any release ABI-compatible with the one its
bindings were generated from, which shares its soname. Once its side campaign has ported
part of the library, the crate bundles the C that remains, with its symbols prefixed, so
that it never collides with another copy of the library in the same process, and passes
the prefix to the C builds of the campaigns that depend on it, as the raw bindings'
Generation section describes.

## 4. Sources

A library the target links from the system has no
source of the campaign's own, so its side campaign's `c/` is the library's upstream
repository at the release the target was built against: the version its build resolved,
as its build system reports it (CMake's found version, `pkg-config --modversion`), the
system package that provides it, or, for a library built from source, its own version
header. The distribution's patches to that release, if any, are recorded beside it, in the
library's `resolved` and `source` in `dependencies.json`.

parent, under its own `crustify/builds/<variant>/install`, so that each variant of the
target links the library built with the same instrumentation; a sanitizer that instruments
every component, MSan among them, needs it. The parent's variants are then rebuilt against
those installs, as the setup workflow's Builds section describes.

on the system's glibc, so the target keeps linking it, and its side campaign's `c/` holds
glibc's source at the installed version, for reading its behaviour. Its raw bindings, like
any wrapper's, are generated from the host's headers, which are that glibc's, so layouts and
constants that differ between architectures, such as `struct stat`, are the campaign
target's.

Before a campaign creates a library's wrapper, it checks `crustify-rs` for
`<source>-crustify`. One that exists is cloned and its side campaign continued: what it
already wraps is not scheduled again, and only what it lacks is planned, as additions to
its own plan. A library without one gets a new repository, created once the user approves,
which every later campaign that uses the library continues.

entities a subsystem, a header's API or a kind of resource (sockets, memory maps,
processes) groups, never for an item or two: entities that share state, such as a stream's

would have put none.

  show. Same behaviour is not required: a port is a new implementation, and a difference
  the port can absorb in its own safe code (a verifier, a loop in place of a sizing call,
  configuration loaded eagerly), or that it can adopt deliberately and record as the safe
  API's changed behaviour (an option it rejects, a deprecated fallback it drops), weighs

  note says, citing the release point after which the C stops sharing it. A crate that
  binds the C library and exposes its raw handles can; one that reimplements the library
  serves only where no state crosses to the remaining C, as
  [Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) describes. An entity
  only one module uses, whose port keeps the state in Rust, shares none;

  behaviour reachable from its safe API, by the hazards
  [`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary excludes from the campaign's
  own; a deterministic scan of its unsafe surface backs the judgement where that surface
  is large or the judgement is borderline;

  advisories: its release history and its maintainers, weighed by how much the crate does
  and how settled its scope is, since a complete crate with a narrow scope needs few
  releases. A crate whose `-sys` crate the alternative route would use anyway is no

those entities get no wrapper and no batches: their consumers use the crate directly, and

pull request opened with the user's approval, so that the fork can be dropped once it is
merged.
<!-- TODO: whether a ship point may pin an unmerged fork is decided at the end of the

crustify campaign's.

batch that binds or ports one of its users checks the route against the code it translates,
by the uses the entity's `match` and note describe, and reports what it found in its final
message, which is recorded as the entity's `confirmation`. Each later batch takes
the confirmed route.

only a crate the user has not adopted would, the batch reports it, and it is put
to the user, whose answer is recorded among the decision's `overrides`.

# Binding symbols

How a scheduled C symbol becomes a safe Rust binding: the symbol route, which follows
[`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section and reaches the types
[`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md) binds. [`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md) starts from it.

## 1. Functions

A function is bound as a `pub fn`; it is a `pub unsafe fn` only when no safe type-level
contract can express its caller obligation. Its FFI call, and the raw pointers it
reconstructs for it, sit in its module's `ffi_import` region, as the
[conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes.

Its signature follows the analysis's findings, each argument and return taking the safe
form of what it names:

- **Out-parameters.** A pointer the function only writes through, to hand back a result,
  is part of the return, several of them a tuple, present only in the outcome in which the
  function writes it.
- **Buffers.** A pointer and the count that bounds it are one slice, the count taken from
  it; a buffer the function fills returns the part it filled.
- **Strings.** A NUL-terminated string the function borrows for the call is a borrowed C
  string, or the Rust string or path type of the encoding the analysis establishes,
  converted at the call, an interior NUL rejected before it. A returned string is a borrow
  tied to what keeps it alive, or an owner over its releaser where the caller frees it.
- **Nullability.** A nullable pointer is an `Option`.
- **Errors.** A function that can fail returns a `Result`, its failure read from the error
  convention the analysis establishes: a status return, a sentinel return, or error state
  the library keeps beside the call, read immediately after it, before another call into
  the library can replace it. Error state a failure sets and only a caller clears, such as
  a sticky error flag, tells the call's failure by its change alone, with nothing else able
  to change it in between. A return that reports only success is not returned, and an
  outcome its C callers treat as ordinary, such as an exhausted iteration or an absent
  entry, is part of the success value. Each error convention has one error type, carrying
  what the convention reports, `errno`'s being `std::io::Error`.
- **Variadics.** A variadic function is bound through fixed-arity forms: one that formats
  its arguments takes the formatted message, passed to a `"%s"` format, and any other is
  one function per argument list its callers use. A `va_list` function is reached only
  through its variadic sibling.

A `static inline` function a header defines is bound as an exported one is: it is
allowlisted, and called through the raw binding generated for it, as
[`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Generation section describes. The exception is a short
one whose whole implementation is in the header, which may be ported instead, to save the
cost of an FFI call, unless what it does depends on the build's features or configuration.
A reimplementation is a port, as [`porting`](../../porting/SKILL.md) describes, and is
annotated `Replaces`, as the [conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Anchors section describes.

Moved (exclusively or refcounted), borrowed (immutably or mutably), nullable, scalar and
array variants are separate functions when one signature cannot express every valid
contract. A function taking or returning type-erased arguments is generic.

A method is emitted in an `impl T` block on the type it implements, taking `&self` or
`&mut self` as its first argument. A free function stays free.

## 2. Globals

A global is bound as a `'static` borrow, never as an owner, its value taking the safe form
its type takes in a signature, as [Functions](#1-functions) describes. Its access
discipline follows from every C access:

- immutable after initialization: a shared handle;
- synchronized by C: the matching safe synchronization (an atomic, or guards handing out
  the shared or exclusive handle under the lock), never discarding a lock's status;
- otherwise mutable: `unsafe` accessors that exclude concurrent access, reported as such;
- thread-local: a handle borrowed for a closure on the current thread, neither `Send` nor
  `Sync`.

The accesses that decide are those the C declaration's contract allows, not only those the
campaign's C makes, since the crate cannot see every program it is linked into. A global
the library documents as one a program may set, such as libc's standard streams, is
otherwise mutable, however the C the campaign sees uses it. Where such a global holds a
pointer, the C that closes or reassigns it may free what it pointed to, so the accessor is
`unsafe`, its caller vouching for the lifetime it chooses.

A lock counts only if every access takes it and it rejects same-thread re-entry. A global
C sets up in a routine, rather than in its definition, is reached through the safe API only
once that routine has run, however the binding ensures it.

## 3. Function pointers

A function pointer is bound from its declaration and every site that calls it or supplies
it, a function assigned to it or passed as it. One a typedef declares is named after its
typedef; one written inline is named after the site that declares it, the field,
parameter, return or global, as the [conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Naming
section describes, so that two inline pointers of one signature in one file are two items
when their sites differ.
<!-- TODO: wavefront keys an inline function pointer by its signature and home file, so
the sites of one signature in one file are one item; it has yet to key them by declaring
site, a local's or a cast's folded into the site whose value it carries. -->

It is bound to a safe callable type that holds either of its implementations:

- a Rust closure, which C reaches through a trampoline of the C signature and the context
  C passes back to it; and
- a C function, with its context, which Rust calls: made only inside the crate, through an
  `unsafe` constructor whose contract states what the C that supplies it guarantees, the
  function's validity and its context's lifetime and threads, and safe to call, its
  arguments and result converted as a function's binding converts them.

A function pointer that crosses the boundary gets both, whichever direction its uses take
today, since a port turns the C that calls or supplies it into Rust, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section describes, and its safe API
does not change then. Its consumers see only the safe form, its closures taking and
returning safe types: a closure borrowed for the call, `impl FnMut(…)`, where C keeps it
for the call that receives it; an owned closure, released with its context, where C keeps
it until it releases it; and a trait, for a struct of function pointers a library calls
into, which Rust types and the C implementation implement alike. A function pointer read
from C, such as a field's getter returns, is the callable type, never the raw pointer.
How long C keeps it is a finding of the analysis.

Its trampoline is a panic barrier, which maps a panic to the C's error convention, and it
refuses a re-entrant call, which would alias an `FnMut` closure, unless the analysis shows
that C re-enters it, which takes an `Fn` closure instead. A function pointer C calls from
another thread takes a `Send` closure, and a `Sync` one when C may call it from several at
once. Four cases shape the type further:

- one without a context parameter carries no captured state: its Rust implementation is a
  closure without captures, each closure type its own trampoline, or a plain function;
- one C reads as absent when null, where it uses a default or calls nothing, is an
  `Option` of the callable type;
- one C compares with a known function, such as its default implementation, keeps in its C
  variant the pointer it was made from, so that the comparison still holds; and
- one whose context C reaches through another argument, such as the object it is handed,
  has a C half only for functions sound with any such argument. A C function that reads its
  context there is reached only through the object that holds it, by the routine that
  dispatches it with that object, bound or ported, which calls it through its raw binding,
  and never as the callable type, whose safe call could hand it another object. Such a
  function is stored only from C, or through an `unsafe` setter whose contract carries the
  object's context, and is read back as its address, no callable.

A function that calls a callback with an object it is working on lends that object to the
callback. The analysis establishes which of the object's routines C allows from within the
callback. One it does not allow, such as the function itself or one that resets the state
the function resumes from, is refused there by the binding, since the callback holds an
exclusive handle the borrow checker cannot tell from any other.

When its sites hand ownership across differently, each distribution has its own distinctly
named callable type over the one C function-pointer type.

## 4. Macros

A C macro is bound to a Rust form of its own:

- a type-generating macro, to one generic type, through [`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md),
  its instances aliases of it;
- a constant macro, to a `const`, defined from its generated binding;
- a symbol alias, through the safe wrapper of the symbol it names, each of whose stand-ins
  stands in for the alias too and carries its anchor beside the symbol's own: where the
  symbol is a lifecycle primitive, the strategy methods that call it, as
  [Lifecycle strategies](#5-lifecycle-strategies) describes; and
- a macro that implements logic, to a function, `#[inline]`, or `const` where its body
  computes on its arguments alone, which reimplements the body and reaches C only for the
  symbols its expansion uses, through their safe wrappers, and for the fields it accesses,
  through their accessors. A `macro_rules!` takes its place only where a function cannot
  express it: control flow that leaves its caller, token pasting or stringification, an
  argument used as a place, or one evaluated lazily or more than once.

A macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration, which the Rust does not see,
is the exception: it is reached through a shim, `crustify_<NAME>`, bound and wrapped.

## 5. Lifecycle strategies

A type's own lifecycle routines are bound with the type, as
[`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section describes. The foundational
modules hold the rest: the allocators or constructors, releasers, disposers and cloners of
type-erased memory and of strings, each with the lifecycle role established while
planning, as [`decomposition`](../../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational
modules section describes. The analysis confirms each role from the item's body, and a role
the body contradicts is corrected, the correction recorded with the batch.

In a foundational module's batch, an item with a lifecycle role becomes a generic policy
or strategy that calls the primitive, through which the owners of strings and of
type-erased singletons and arrays allocate, clone and release what they hold, so that each
owner frees what it holds through the family that allocated it. The primitive itself is
not also exposed as an ordinary safe function. The module's other items follow their
route.

Singleton and array handles have separate policies, each in its primitive's home. A
family's allocator, releaser and cloner form one policy. A releaser that frees a container together with its
elements is no policy of the container: where its body only releases each element and then
the container, the owner holds its elements as their own owners, under the container's
allocator's policy, and releases as the releaser does without calling it; where it does
more, the owner is hand-written.

  arguments and result converted as a function's binding converts them.

A function pointer that crosses the boundary gets both, whichever direction its uses take
today, since a port turns the C that calls or supplies it into Rust, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section describes, and its safe API
does not change then. Its consumers see only the safe form, its closures taking and
returning safe types: a closure borrowed for the call, `impl FnMut(…)`, where C keeps it
for the call that receives it; an owned closure, released with its context, where C keeps
it until it releases it; and a trait, for a struct of function pointers a library calls
into, which Rust types and the C implementation implement alike. A function pointer read
from C, such as a field's getter returns, is the callable type, never the raw pointer.
How long C keeps it is a finding of the analysis.

Its trampoline is a panic barrier, which maps a panic to the C's error convention, and it
refuses a re-entrant call, which would alias an `FnMut` closure, unless the analysis shows
that C re-enters it, which takes an `Fn` closure instead. A function pointer C calls from
another thread takes a `Send` closure, and a `Sync` one when C may call it from several at
once. Four cases shape the type further:

- one without a context parameter carries no captured state: its Rust implementation is a
  closure without captures, each closure type its own trampoline, or a plain function;
- one C reads as absent when null, where it uses a default or calls nothing, is an
  `Option` of the callable type;
- one C compares with a known function, such as its default implementation, keeps in its C
  variant the pointer it was made from, so that the comparison still holds; and
- one whose context C reaches through another argument, such as the object it is handed,
  has a C half only for functions sound with any such argument. A C function that reads its
  context there is reached only through the object that holds it, by the routine that
  dispatches it with that object, bound or ported, which calls it through its raw binding,
  and never as the callable type, whose safe call could hand it another object. Such a
  function is stored only from C, or through an `unsafe` setter whose contract carries the
  object's context, and is read back as its address, no callable.

A function that calls a callback with an object it is working on lends that object to the
callback. The analysis establishes which of the object's routines C allows from within the
callback. One it does not allow, such as the function itself or one that resets the state
the function resumes from, is refused there by the binding, since the callback holds an
exclusive handle the borrow checker cannot tell from any other.

When its sites hand ownership across differently, each distribution has its own distinctly
named callable type over the one C function-pointer type.

## 4. Macros

A C macro is bound to a Rust form of its own:

- a type-generating macro, to one generic type, through [`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md),
  its instances aliases of it;
- a constant macro, to a `const`, defined from its generated binding;
- a symbol alias, through the safe wrapper of the symbol it names, each of whose stand-ins
  stands in for the alias too and carries its anchor beside the symbol's own: where the
  symbol is a lifecycle primitive, the strategy methods that call it, as
  [Lifecycle strategies](#5-lifecycle-strategies) describes; and
- a macro that implements logic, to a function, `#[inline]`, or `const` where its body
  computes on its arguments alone, which reimplements the body and reaches C only for the
  symbols its expansion uses, through their safe wrappers, and for the fields it accesses,
  through their accessors. A `macro_rules!` takes its place only where a function cannot
  express it: control flow that leaves its caller, token pasting or stringification, an
  argument used as a place, or one evaluated lazily or more than once.

A macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration, which the Rust does not see,
is the exception: it is reached through a shim, `crustify_<NAME>`, bound and wrapped.

## 5. Lifecycle strategies

A type's own lifecycle routines are bound with the type, as
[`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section describes. The foundational
modules hold the rest: the allocators or constructors, releasers, disposers and cloners of
type-erased memory and of strings, each with the lifecycle role established while
planning, as [`decomposition`](../../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational
modules section describes. The analysis confirms each role from the item's body, and a role
the body contradicts is corrected, the correction recorded with the batch.

In a foundational module's batch, an item with a lifecycle role becomes a generic policy
or strategy that calls the primitive, through which the owners of strings and of
type-erased singletons and arrays allocate, clone and release what they hold, so that each
owner frees what it holds through the family that allocated it. The primitive itself is
not also exposed as an ordinary safe function. The module's other items follow their
route.

Singleton and array handles have separate policies, each in its primitive's home. A
family's allocator, releaser and cloner form one policy. A releaser that frees a container together with its
elements is no policy of the container: where its body only releases each element and then
the container, the owner holds its elements as their own owners, under the container's
allocator's policy, and releases as the releaser does without calling it; where it does
more, the owner is hand-written.

name: porting
description: "How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust: its native API, its later stages, the FFI boundary and its exports, and the routes porting-types and porting-symbols give types and symbols. Read before porting any item, and when reviewing ports."
---

# Porting

How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust. A port starts from the item's
analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes, and keeps C interoperability
and observable behaviour for as long as C consumes the item. A type takes the type route,
for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`porting-types`](types/SKILL.md) describes; a
symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, static inline functions
and macros, as [`porting-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

A port gives an item its native safe API at once, and that API does not change after it.
An item the remaining C still uses keeps a C form behind it, its C layout, its storage in
C's allocator, its export or its integer values, so that the C keeps working while its
Rust consumers stay agnostic of which form implements it. The later stages its kind
describes below migrate that form to Rust, part by part, once the switches that free
it have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section schedules them. An item no C uses is native in its API and its implementation from
its port.

A later stage changes the item and the code inside the crate that reaches its C form, in
its module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions
section describes, never the safe API its consumers use, and keeps the item's tests
passing. A stage that moves state out of C, a lock or a handle a type held in its C layout,
or memory C's allocator held, moves its uses onto the standard library where
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section lets it.

## 1. FFI boundary

`binding`'s Safe boundary section applies to a port unchanged. When a wrapper of the item
already exists, because a module that ran before needed it, the port keeps that wrapper's
safe API and replaces only what is behind it, so that its consumers do not change, as do
its later stages. A standard-library operation is used directly when it is equivalent and
no C-interoperability requirement remains, an out-of-tree library's entity included, as
`binding`'s Safe boundary section describes.

While C consumers remain, a ported item is re-exported to C as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes:

- The raw gateway, its module's `ffi_export` region, reconstructs safe wrappers and calls
  the native function.
- The gateway is compiled only under its module's export feature, which stays off until
  the module switches, so that the exports never collide with the C they replace.
- At the switch, the Rust static library is linked in place of the TU through the actual
  build system, without assuming link mechanics, and the TU is deleted, as
  [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes.

How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust. A port starts from the item's
analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes, and keeps C interoperability
and observable behaviour for as long as C consumes the item. A type takes the type route,
for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`porting-types`](types/SKILL.md) describes; a
symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, static inline functions
and macros, as [`porting-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

A port gives an item its native safe API at once, and that API does not change after it.
An item the remaining C still uses keeps a C form behind it, its C layout, its storage in
C's allocator, its export or its integer values, so that the C keeps working while its
Rust consumers stay agnostic of which form implements it. The later stages its kind
describes below migrate that form to Rust, part by part, once the switches that free
it have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section schedules them. An item no C uses is native in its API and its implementation from
its port.

its module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions
section describes, never the safe API its consumers use, and keeps the item's tests
passing. A stage that moves state out of C, a lock or a handle a type held in its C layout,

[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section lets it.

When the type system should reject a program, the test is a compile-fail doctest or a
`trybuild` case.

## 2. Equivalence tests

Equivalence tests run the C and the Rust that translates it on independently owned inputs
built from one description, and compare:

- return values and errors;
- out-parameters and buffers;
- callbacks;
- state transitions; and
- lifecycle effects.

They use multi-call sequences and compare after each step; single calls are only a
baseline.

The C side of a test meets the preconditions the C sets its callers, as the wrapper meets
them before its own calls: a library's global initialisation, which writes state its
routines read without synchronisation, runs before the test's first call that reads it,
since the harness runs other tests beside it on other threads.

They compare what the C specifies, through the mapping the safe API applies to it, such as
its status returns as errors and its null pointers as absent values, and not what it leaves
unspecified, such as an iteration order, a message's text, a pointer's value or an
allocation count. A confirmed C defect is not copied into Rust. The divergence is
documented, equivalence tests are retained for the unaffected behaviour, and the
corrected-behaviour regression is a unit test.

`equiv_pub` holds the module's exported API to the C strictly. `equiv_priv` compares an
internal routine with its C counterpart only where one exists, since an idiomatic port may
restructure the internals; a C function the raw bindings do not reach, one with internal
linkage, is compared through the functions that call it. A macro that implements
logic is compared where it expands, through the functions that hold its expansions, since a
test of their callers compares the callers' logic, not the macro's. When no function the
raw bindings reach runs any of its expansions, directly or through the functions it calls,
no equivalence test compares it: its unit tests check it against the replacement list at
each expansion site's arguments, and the batch reports the sites as unreached, until the
port of the module that holds them compares them.

In a port, equivalence tests are the evidence of a module's migration. While its waves run,
the variants still build its C, which they reach through the raw bindings while the ported
Rust runs under its own names; at its switch they are retired with the C, and the
module evolves as Rust from then on, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes. Only its exports still keep the C contract, which the C tests that stay check.

# Item analysis

How a scheduled C item is analysed before it is bound or ported. The analysis is the same
for both: what it establishes shapes the binding or port that follows.

## 1. Scope

Each item is analysed from its source declarations and definitions, its dependency closure,
its callers, its field touchers and its existing Rust consumers. For every pointer field,
argument and return, every code path that stores, transfers, clones, retains or frees it is
inspected.

## 2. Findings

The analysis establishes:

- ownership and transfer direction;
- shared or mutable access;
- nullability;
- scalar, array, or other cardinality;
- type erasure and known element types;
- borrow and keepalive relationships;
- address retention: whether C keeps an object's address beyond the call that receives it,
  to read it, call back with it or free it;
- construction, clone, and destruction paths;
- states and transitions: the states each type's objects pass through, and the calls that
  move them between states, in the orders C allows, with the calls a callback may make on
  the object its caller lends it, and those that would corrupt the caller's state;
- out-parameters: the pointer arguments a function only writes through;
- string encodings, where a string is known to hold text or a path; and
- failure reporting: the status or sentinel returns and the error state beside the call
  through which a function fails, and the outcomes its callers treat as ordinary.

Observed behaviour overrides names and comments. A distinction the analysis establishes is
preserved in Rust rather than flattened into a copy of an ambiguous C signature.

**Verdict: approved, with no fixes required.** The change does not weaken a check. I changed and landed nothing, made no scratch, and ran no gate or rerun, as you asked.

I reviewed crustify `769d102` against `215a692`: one paragraph added to the end of `porting-symbols`' Macros section. It touches no protected path.

**Review section checks**
- **Evidence:** it holds. `c/src/util/strnlen.h` has the two branches the proposal describes, and both return the same length for every input. The task message for `wave-225/batch-0` says "Port what this build defines…" (`task.md:20`). The module pass, `wave-225/batch-1`, flagged the same ambiguity in the shim exception and filed no finding. `dependencies.json` records the `std` route as confirmed by `wave-225/batch-0`.
- **The change answers the signal:** yes. It covers the evidence's second half: the shim is kept only where the branches compute different results. It leaves open the first half, which kinds of configuration the exception means (see the first non-required item).
- **Goals:** Idiomatic Rust and Least constraint are named, and the change serves both.
- **Placement and wording:** the paragraph sits in the right section, uses none of libgit2's names, and keeps its reason, as `authoring` asks.
- **Validation:** the batch produced exactly the native port the rule now prescribes, and the module pass judged it. The proposal says plainly that the `NO_STRNLEN` branch is checked by reading only. That is accurate.
- **Record row:** the recurrence signal is something a campaign would observe. `watched` is the right status, since no test checks the rule.

**Consistency with the other skills that cover the same thing.** I found no contradiction.
- **`binding-symbols`' Macros section:** the shim exception still applies to a port. It is only narrowed to macros whose branches compute different results, and "keeps the shim `binding-symbols` gives it" defers to that section.
- **`binding-symbols`' static inline exception:** it is binding-only, and a port already ports static inline functions under `porting-symbols`' Static inline functions section.
- **`bindgen`'s Extending section:** a shim "only for" a configuration-dependent macro is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one, so it still holds.
- **`porting`'s FFI boundary section:** the last sentence applies its standard-library rule to aliases. That also settles the literal reading of `binding-symbols`' "the safe wrapper of the symbol it names", which the evidence shows a run tripped on.
- **`dependencies`' Routes and Confirmation sections:** both are cited correctly. They decide how the aliased library entity is reached, and nothing more.
- **`porting-symbols`' Functions section:** "C only an unbuilt configuration compiles is no remaining C" agrees with naming the branches the build does not take.
- **`testing`' rule that a macro is compared where it expands:** unchanged.

**Does it weaken a check, and who establishes that every configuration computes the same?**
- **No check is loosened:** no test, gate, lint, review objective or tool detection. The built configuration's equivalence tests still compare the port with the C's own expansion. The other branches were never built or tested by the campaign, before or after.
- **What changes:** on configurations the campaign never builds, the C's own expansion was correct by construction. That is replaced by a judgement made by reading.
- **Who makes that judgement:** `dependencies` does not; it only gives the alias's route. The rule leaves it to the porter, implicitly. The module pass reads it, because the documentation must name the branches not taken, which is what `wave-225/batch-1` did.
- **What no one can do:** prove a wrong judgement as a finding on this host. The `equiv` reproducer in `reviewing` needs the raw C running, and the unbuilt branch is not built. The `logic` sources of a specification do not include that branch's C.

**Not required (they do not affect the verdict)**
1. The change does not say which kinds of configuration the shim exception means: a target platform, which Rust's `cfg` can see, or a feature it cannot. The proposal's Evidence says the section should say this. Settling it would add a rule. Otherwise the Evidence could drop that claim.
2. The rule could name the analysis as what establishes that the branches agree, and have the documentation say why they agree, not just name the other branches. Either would add a rule.
3. The colon clause ("a port reimplements the body, and a shim over the C's expansion would make it a binding") reads as if it explains why the differing macro keeps its shim. In fact it explains why the same-result macro gets none. A rewording would fix it. Removing the clause would also work, but `authoring` asks that a rule keep its reason, so a rewording is better.
4. The second mention of `binding-symbols` is not linked. The rest of the file links that skill each time it names it.
5. The proposal names its goals but not the measure of each goal it expects to move, which `evolution`'s Proposals section asks for. Least constraint's per-module count of rules a task message had to settle would fit.
6. One gap predates this change and is not created by it: a macro that keeps its shim in a port still calls C. No skill says what happens to that shim once its header goes away with the last C file that includes it.
